claims.text: The initial eutectic high-entropy alloy has dual-phase lamellar colonies containing a continuous hard B2 phase interwoven with a softer phase.
Internal boundaries associated with the continuous hard phase are preferred sites for microcrack initiation during tensile deformation.
Isothermal annealing can transform an initially continuous B2 matrix.
The proposed annealing treatment will convert the continuous hard B2 phase into discrete coherent precipitates within a continuous ductile BCC or FCC matrix.
Annealing at approximately 600 °C for 120 hours is a suitable treatment for producing the proposed microstructural inversion.
Breaking the continuous hard phase into isolated precipitates will reduce stress concentrations at internal boundaries.
The inverted microstructure will improve dislocation transmission through the ductile matrix.
Reduced phase connectivity and lower boundary stress concentrations will suppress microcrack initiation and propagation.
Discrete coherent precipitates will impede dislocation motion and provide precipitation strengthening.
The annealed alloy will have greater room-temperature tensile ductility than the as-cast lamellar baseline.
The annealed alloy will maintain or slightly increase yield strength relative to the as-cast lamellar baseline.
The conventional as-cast lamellar baseline is strong but exhibits brittle room-temperature tensile behavior because microcracks initiate at internal boundaries.
The proposed effect is applicable to AlCoCrFeNi2.1 or related eutectic high-entropy alloys with initially continuous lamellar microstructures.
The beneficial effect requires a composition capable of separating into the desired discrete-precipitate microstructure.
Excessive precipitate coarsening during annealing may degrade strength.
Post-annealing defects could compromise the beneficial mechanical response.
The exact transformation kinetics and mechanical-property changes will vary with alloy composition and processing conditions.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing identically prepared baseline and 600 °C/120-hour annealed batches using microscopy and room-temperature tensile testing.
Failure to obtain the proposed precipitate morphology, or failure to improve ductility while at least maintaining yield strength, would falsify the hypothesis.
